subject: Post-demo: Streaming buyflow performance details & next steps

Subject: Post-demo: Streaming buyflow performance details & next steps

Hi Sara / Acme Platform team,

Thanks again for the demo time today — useful signal on the streaming buyflow and how you expect partials to drive the UX. Quick recap + asks so we can size a recommendation for Dedicated/Private and call out any risks against your latency targets.

Recap from the call:
- Workload: low-latency streaming for a "buyflow" assistant (audio -> ASR -> LLM streaming responses back to client).
- Latency SLO discussed: target p95 end-to-end for first partial ~200ms, steady p95 for subsequent partials ~150-250ms depending on chunk size.
- Concurrency: you mentioned 35–50 steady concurrent streams per region, with marketing-led spikes up to ~140–160 concurrent for short windows (5–12 minutes).
- Token velocity: ~20–30 tokens/sec per active stream on average; peaks up to 60 tokens/sec for noisy sessions.
- Typical request length: partials every 250–500ms; full turn ~800–1200 tokens.

Action items for sizing (can you confirm and attach if available):
1) A short CSV with 24h telemetry (timestamp, concurrent_streams, tokens_emitted/sec) — I attached a sample template and filled placeholders (acme_stream_profile.csv).
2) Which regions these streams originate from and whether cross-region fallback is acceptable.
3) Max allowed latency for the business-critical path (is 200ms p95 a hard requirement or aspirational?).
4) Any regulatory constraints on data residency or on-prem requirements.

Next steps from Redwood: Marcus + Vanessa will draft a baseline sizing and a low-latency config (batching, KV cache, recommended instance shapes) and a short SLA table for the pilot. Expect a first-pass by tomorrow EOD PT.

Attachments: acme_stream_profile.csv (sample template)

Thanks — talk soon.

—
Soojin Lee
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
soojin@redwood.com

On Tue, Aug 10, 2027 at 2:07 PM Soojin Lee <soojin@redwood.com> wrote:
> Hi Sara / Acme Platform team,

> Thanks again for the demo time today — useful signal on the streaming buyflow and how you expect partials to drive the UX. Quick recap + asks so we can size a recommendation for Dedicated/Private and call out any risks against your latency targets.

Thanks Soojin — great summary. Attaching a 24h extract from our staging telemetry (acme_stream_profile.csv). Key clarifications below:

- Regions: streams come primarily from us-west1 (70%) and us-east1 (25%) with occasional eu-west1 traffic (5%). For pilot we can keep the test footprint in us-west1 only.
- True steady concurrency is ~38 average during business hours, 22 overnight. Marketing campaigns last week gave us two spikes: 152 concurrent at 11:14AM and 139 concurrent at 15:02PM, both ~6–9 minute durations.
- Token velocity: median 24 tokens/sec, 95th percentile 58 tokens/sec across streams.
- Partial frequency: client sends audio chunks that result in partials every ~300ms; the UI applies the first partial immediately.
- Hard constraints: consumer UX requires first partial visible within 250ms p95; anything above 350ms will degrade conversion noticeably.

Questions for Redwood:
1) Can you support per-request streaming partials with p95 <= 250ms in us-west1 under the peak concurrency above?
2) Any recommendations on max tokens/window we should cap at to avoid model stalls?
3) Is there a simple fallback plan (lower-quality quantized model) you suggest if we hit capacity limits during spikes?

Attaching: acme_stream_profile.csv

—
Sara Johnson
Head of Product, Acme AI
sara.johnson@acme.ai

From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin@redwood.com>, Sara Johnson <sara.johnson@acme.ai>, Platform Eng <platform@acme.ai>
Cc: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 11 Aug 2027 08:55:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-demo: Streaming buyflow performance details & next steps

Thanks for the telemetry, Sara — helpful. I ran a quick sizing pass against the profile and here are engineering notes / preliminary recommendations.

Summary of constraints (from your data):- steady concurrency: 38 (business hours)- peak concurrency: 152 (short bursts)- median token/sec per stream: 24; 95th: 58- partial interval: ~300ms

Prelim Redwood recommendation for pilot (us-west1):
- Serving profile: dedicate a small pool of low-latency instances (recommended: 4 x GPU nodes, each with 80GB A100 or equivalent). These nodes would be configured for streaming-optimized execution paths (reduced batching window, aggressive KV cache reuse).
- Concurrency handling: target per-node max concurrent streams ~40 for low-latency. 4 nodes => comfortable steady-state (40*4=160) with headroom for short bursts; autoscale policy: scale +1 node on sustained >70% utilization for 2 minutes, with burst buffer for 10-minute windows.
- Latency expectation: under the above config and with small batching (batch window <= 25ms) we estimate first-partial p95 ~180–240ms depending on on-host noise; subsequent partials ~120–200ms.
- Token throughput: per-node sustained throughput estimate ~1,000–1,500 tokens/sec for streaming workloads (depends on model size/quantization); cluster aggregate 4k–6k tokens/sec.
- Fallbacks: recommend a quantized model variant (8-bit) as a warm fallback; Redwood runtime can auto-fall back by routing policy when cluster utilization >85%. This will reduce latency variability but may slightly affect output quality.

Open questions / asks from Acme to finalize sizing:
1) Confirm which model variant you want for pilot (large-llm-v1 vs large-llm-v1-8q). Model choice materially changes tokens/sec numbers.
2) Max allowed token/stream window before you consider truncation (we assume 1,200 tokens per turn as a starting point).
3) Does the client tolerate micro-batching at 20–25ms windows? If not, we can reduce but cost increases.

I've attached a short SLA table that maps config -> expected p95 ranges (redwood_sla_table.pdf). If that looks reasonable, we can convert to a formal Mutual Action Plan and draft a PO for Dedicated pilot capacity.

Propose a 30-minute technical scoping tomorrow at 10:00am PT to lock model choice and autoscale thresholds — if that works for you, I'll send a calendar invite.

—
Marcus Lin
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime
